options.text: Replicas converge only if writes eventually stop
The system behaves like one up-to-date copy: once a write completes, later reads see that write or a newer one
Transactions run one at a time in some serial order

questions.explanation: Linearizability is a recency guarantee on single objects: the system appears to have a single up-to-date copy, and reads never see stale data once a write completes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about linearizability vs serializability is correct?

options.text: They are two words for the same thing
Linearizability is single-object recency (real-time order); serializability is transaction isolation (some serial order). They are independent.

questions.explanation: Linearizability concerns real-time recency of single-object operations; serializability concerns transactions appearing to run in some serial order. Both together is strict serializability.

questions.prompt: Which consistency model is the strongest that still stays highly available during a network partition?

options.text: No consistency is available during a partition

questions.explanation: Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect ordering and can remain available under partition, unlike linearizability which requires coordination.

questions.prompt: Is the 'C' in ACID the same as the 'C' in CAP?

options.text: Yes, both mean the same consistency
No — ACID's C is application integrity constraints; CAP's C is linearizability

questions.explanation: They are different ideas: ACID's C is about the integrity constraints the application defines; CAP's C is linearizability, a replication recency guarantee.

questions.prompt: Match each consistency guarantee to its promise.

pairs.right: You always see your own most recent writes
Successive reads never go backward in time
Reads always see the latest write, as if one copy

questions.explanation: Each guarantee targets a specific anomaly: seeing your own writes, not moving backward, eventual convergence, or full real-time recency.

questions.prompt: A 'is this username taken?' check must never let two people claim the same name. Which model does it need?
questions.explanation: Uniqueness requires seeing the very latest state so only one claimant wins — that is linearizability. Eventual consistency could let both succeed.
